entries.title: How do the US midterms work, and why are they so important for Trump's presidency?
entries.summary: US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.
entries.content:
United States of America

US midterms: What you need to know

October 28, 2026

US voters are electing a new Congress. The results will be decisive for the future of the United States, and a judgment on Donald Trump's second term as president.

On November 3, United States citizens will vote in the midterm elections. These won't decide who gets to sit in the White House; instead, Americans will be voting on who they want to see in the Capitol.

Midterm elections are held every four years, at the exact halfway point between presidential elections. The people of the United States decide who will represent them in the two chambers of the US Congress, the House of Representatives and the Senate. Some states are also voting for their governor. These are the decisions on the ballot paper — but they are not the only thing voters will be taking into account.

J. Miles Coleman, an election analyst at the Center for Politics at the University of Virginia, explained before the last midterms that they were "often a referendum on the president and party currently in power." If the people are content, the party of the leader in the White House does better than if the people are predominantly dissatisfied. President Donald Trump's approval ratings are currently at a record low.

Who are Americans electing in the midterms?

All the seats in the US House of Representatives are up for election. Its 435 members are elected by eligible voters across the country. Each member represents one electoral district. These are allocated based on population size. As a result, relatively large US states where few people live, such as Wyoming, have only one seat in the House of Representatives. New Jersey, a much smaller state by surface area but with a larger population, has 12. Representatives are elected for a two-year term of office.

US senators, on the other hand, are elected for a six-year term. The Senate, the other chamber of the US Congress, has 100 seats: two for each of the 50 US states, regardless of size. Around one third of these senatorial seats come up for election every two years. This year there are 35, meaning that not every state will be electing a senator in these midterms.

Separately, voters in 36 states will elect their governor, whose term of office is four years in most states. Many decisions in the US are taken at state level, on everything from abortion law to education and electoral procedure. It can therefore make a considerable difference to people's lives whether Democrats or Republicans are the ones making these decisions in their state.

Who currently has a majority in the US Congress?

At present, the Republicans, the party of President Trump, have a majority in both houses of Congress — but its margin is slim.

The House of Representatives currently has 218 Republican deputies, 214 Democrats, and one independent, who usually votes with the Republicans. Two seats are vacant. Observers think it likely that the Democrats will seize the majority in this chamber in the upcoming elections. "It would be a surprise if the Democrats don't at least take the House [of Representatives]," Coleman told the American broadcaster CBS at the end of October.

In the Senate there are currently 53 Republicans, 45 Democrats, and two independent senators who usually vote with the Democrats. When a vote in the Senate is deadlocked 50:50, the US vice president has the deciding vote. This means that currently, Trump's Vice President JD Vance would tip the scales if there were a tie in a Senate vote.

Why are the midterms so important?

Voter turnout is typically lower for midterms than for presidential elections, but the results will decisively influence US politics for the next few years. Despite the significant executive power delegated to the presidency, the majority of federal political decisions have to be approved by Congress before they can be implemented.

It is therefore considerably easier for Trump to govern the country as he chooses if the Republicans have a majority in both chambers of Congress. If the Democrats win a majority in one or both chambers, it will be more difficult for him to make changes to either domestic or foreign policy.

Which races are crucial?

The Democrats only need to win four more seats in the House of Representatives to gain a majority. They would then have 218 representatives. Out of the 435 races, only a few are still considered toss-ups. These include districts in Iowa, Virginia and Montana.

One senatorial race to watch is the one in Texas. Current polls put Democrat James Talarico level with his Republican rival, Ken Paxton. The Democrats need four more seats in the Senate to win a majority. The possibility that Texas could be one of them is already a sensation. No Democrat has won here at state level since 1994. Talarico now even has the support of some members of the Bush family, the Texas Republican dynasty of former presidents George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush, his son.

In the gubernatorial elections it is possible that, for the first time in US history, a Black woman could become state governor. In Minnesota, the Democrat Amy Klobuchar and the Black Republican Lisa DeMuth are vying for the position, while in Georgia the Black Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms is up against the Republican Rick Jackson.

DeMuth is unlikely to win in Minnesota: The state generally votes Democrat, and Klobuchar, who has been state senator there for almost two decades, is much better known than her rival. In Georgia, however, the latest polls suggest it's neck-and-neck. Bottoms has a realistic chance of winning.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Evacuation from Oleshky: How are preparations going?
entries.summary: A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Preparations underway for Oleshky evacuation

October 28, 2026

A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.

Since a ceasefire took effect in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on October 27, preparations have been underway to evacuate residents trapped there.

Following Russia's occupation of the town in 2022 and the flooding caused by the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023, residents were cut off from the outside world. All access routes to Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River, had been mined. Former Oleshky residents who managed to escape and talked to DW described hunger, no access to medicine, and no electricity or water. About 2,000 people are still living in the town.

According to the Save Ukraine Foundation, it has rescued at least 300 civilians from Oleshky over the past six months. DW spoke with lawyer Myroslava Kharchenko, who works for the organization, about preparations for the upcoming evacuation.

DW: A ceasefire is already in effect in Oleshky. Do you know whether any evacuation efforts have begun?

Myroslava Kharchenko: No, we do not have that information yet. What we do know is that the ceasefire came into effect on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, which is 4 a.m. in Russia. Mine-clearing operations on the road began at around 8 a.m. What is happening inside Oleshky itself, however, is entirely within the military's remit. Everyone involved in this operation has been asked to maintain strict confidentiality. Any careless remark or action could jeopardize the entire evacuation effort.

What I can see is that information is being actively collected through closed internal local chat groups. Registration lists and application forms are being shared, and people are filling them out themselves. Organizers are contacting those who previously requested evacuation to verify details such as their date of birth and current place of residence. They are also asking people to provide contact information for neighbors or relatives who may be nearby or in the same building, because communications are extremely unreliable.

The organizers are also collecting information about the health conditions of those planning to leave. Among them are people who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from recent injuries, including blast and mine-related wounds. We therefore expect those organizing the evacuation to ensure that medical assistance is available for those who need it.

How exactly is the evacuation expected to take place? Will people be evacuated through Russian-controlled territory or via the Dnipro River? Have any routes already been agreed upon?

As far as we know, a river route would be extremely dangerous. We have not heard any confirmation that such an option has been approved. It therefore appears likely that the evacuation route will pass through the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly through Russia before people are able to reach Ukraine. For security reasons, however, none of these details are being made public.

What do you know about the number of people expected to be evacuated?

We are actually very pleased that the evacuation is not expected to take place in a single day. That is important because we hope that those who manage to leave safely during the first stage will serve as an example for others.

People still trapped in Oleshky are extremely afraid. There have already been numerous provocations, and this is not the first attempt to establish such a route or humanitarian corridor.

As a result, there is a great deal of suspicion. Those concerns are based largely on uncertainty, and some people may choose not to leave during the initial phase of the evacuation. Overall, however, we estimate that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated.

How would you assess the role of Melania Trump in making this evacuation possible?

We are immensely grateful to Melania Trump for drawing attention to the humanitarian catastrophe currently unfolding in Oleshky. What is taking place there is in fact genocide committed by the Russian Federation.

We are thankful for her efforts and hope they will help make this evacuation possible. We will be even more grateful once most people are safely removed from the combat zone and arrive in Ukrainian government-controlled territory.

When could the physical evacuation of civilians begin?

I can't say how long it will take. What seems clear, however, is that time will be needed to clear mines from the roads leading into the city. We also understand that many streets inside Oleshky are mined, so additional work will be required to make routes within the city safe.

There is a hospital from which people need to be evacuated. Nearby is a morgue where bodies also need to be recovered.

I do not know whether that will be included as part of this humanitarian corridor, but it is undoubtedly important. The bodies need to be identified and the causes of death established. That process will also take time, regardless of how quickly the military is able to work.

It is difficult to make any predictions because, as you can see, everything is being conducted under strict secrecy. Statements from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides have been extremely cautious, and that is clearly justified under the circumstances.

entries.title: One year on, families seek justice after election violence
entries.summary: One year after Tanzania's deadly post-election violence, families are still seeking answers. A government inquiry recorded 518 deaths. DW research has documented apparent use of excessive force by security forces.
entries.content:
October 28, 2026

One year after Tanzania's deadly post-election violence, families are still seeking answers. A government inquiry recorded 518 deaths. DW research has documented apparent use of excessive force by security forces.

Warning: This article contains descriptions of violence.

For one family member in Mwanza, Tanzania's second-largest city, justice could begin with a simple act: an apology.

Raha, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, said her nephew, who she raised, was killed during protests that erupted following Tanzania's October 2025 general election.

"The government should have asked for forgiveness for what happened. Even just offering condolences," Raha said.

A year later, the family is still waiting for answers about the death of their loved one.

A disputed election, a deadly crackdown

The violence followed an election campaign marked by the exclusion of the main opposition candidate.

Tundu Lissu, leader of the opposition Tanzanian Party for Democracy and Progress, commonly known as Chadema, had been arrested and charged with treason in April 2025 and his party barred from contesting the election.

On election day and in the days that followed, protesters called for political reforms and the resignation of Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

A government-appointed commission, chaired by retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman and commonly referred to as the Chande Commission, found that at least 518 people died from "unnatural causes," many from gunshot wounds, and over 2,000 people were injured.



Othman said the death toll could be higher because some families buried their loved ones without taking their bodies to morgues or reporting to the commission.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) also said the actual number of people killed could be higher.

"It's very clear that it's far more than the 518 people that were presented by the commission," said Oryem Nyeko, HRW's senior Africa researcher.

Police likely acted beyond their guidelines

DW analyzed dozens of videos, interviewed sources, reviewed police guidelines and advocacy research, and obtained a leaked police report.

We could not determine the exact location or publication date of every video, as some of the footage was released later due to internet blackouts or anonymously, for fear of reprisals. However, elements in the footage, our sources, public reports, and an internal police report give strong indications that these videos do reveal pieces of what happened in the days following the election.

The evidence DW has reviewed indicates that police likely acted beyond the scope of their guidelines and training. The material reviewed by DW included cases in which people were killed who were not protesting, where protesters were killed by head wounds, and where protesters were beaten or degraded by people in uniform.

The police's specialized Field Force Unit, identifiable in some footage by its red berets and riot-control equipment, helmets, shields and heavy weapons, appeared repeatedly in the material reviewed by DW.

Separately, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation organization, documented incidents in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's biggest city and commercial capital. In one, the uniformed people are beating civilians with sticks. In another, they are located close to where protesters were shot and killed.



DW also identified incidents in which people who were not protesting appear to have been killed. In Mwanza, videos showed the bodies of young men reportedly killed by people in police uniforms while watching television in a video hall. The case was also cited by Human Rights Watch and flagged by the Chande Commission for further investigation.

Who was responsible?

Tanzania's police guidelines restrict the use of firearms to circumstances where they are absolutely necessary. Yet investigations by DW and human rights organizations documented incidents involving protesters with apparent gunshot wounds to the head and upper body and non-protesters shot while trying to flee or while outside during a government-imposed curfew. 

Security analyst Nicodemus Minde said the commission left crucial questions unanswered.

"The Commission did not really tell us who was responsible and why," he said.

The presence of a police unit at an incident does not establish who ordered an operation or whether senior officials authorized unlawful force.

The Tanzanian President has described the unrest as an attempt to overthrow the government.

DW confronted the Tanzanian government on the allegations of excessive force by police. The Tanzanian Ministry of Home Affairs declined to comment, saying it would interfere with the legal process.

DW also asked the Tanzanian police for comment. No response had been received by the time of publication.

The Chande Commission recommended further investigation but did not identify security bodies, individual officers or commanders who may have been responsible.

A second inquiry, chaired by retired Justice Shaban Ally Lila, began gathering evidence in August 2026 to further investigate. Its findings are still pending.

'There is no justice'

For the family members of those killed, the inquiries have yet to restore trust.

Zuri, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, said her brother and her son were killed in the post-election violence. She asked why the government had not visited affected families.

"We lost our children; we lost our brothers. Why hasn't the government taken any initiative to at least visit us?" Zuri asked.

"They behave as if nothing happened. Is this justice? There is no justice in Tanzania."

entries.title: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors? More of the same is expected, with some small positives predicted.
entries.summary: A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say. Some small positives may be possible though.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

October 28, 2026

A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say. Some small positives may be possible though.

As Israeli politicians begin to try to build a coalition government, after an election that saw no clear winner, response from politicians in surrounding Arab countries has been muted or non-existent.

This may be because, for the time being anyway, it remains unclear as to whether the new Israeli government will continue with "business as usual" under incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or whether a new government headed by Netanyahu's opponents will take what is expected to be a more moderate domestic course.

Whatever the eventual outcome, the consensus is that there is unlikely to be a huge change in Israel's foreign relations with neighboring countries like Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt, and, further afield, the Gulf states. Nor is it likely to produce very different policies toward Palestinians, which many Arab populations in the region feel strongly about.

Both Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot "are two sides of the same coin," Egyptian politician Mostafa Bakry wrote on X after exit polls seemed to indicate an Eisenkot victory (something that's increasingly contested) and Israeli-Arab parties had displaced Netanyahu's far-right allies. "Arab joy at Netanyahu's near-failure to form the government does not mean that what is to come … differs greatly from his predecessor."

"An Eisenkot government would likely be politically fragile, limiting its room for maneuver," Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow in the Middle East and North Africa program at the European Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a commentary last week. "The biggest differences from the current government would be at home: It would halt the judicial overhaul, open a state commission of inquiry into October 7th and pass a conscription law."

However, Oppenheim explained, "when it comes to foreign policy, there would not be a fundamental transformation. Netanyahu's post-October 7th security doctrine — pre-empting threats, operating far beyond Israel's borders and holding 'buffer zones' in neighboring territories — has been embraced by nearly all Jewish Israeli parties."

Palestinian Territories: No two-state solution

One of the election campaign posters for Netanyahu's Likud party bore a stark message — "The right or Palestine" — the message being that if voters did not choose Netanyahu and his right-wing allies, his opponents would be too accommodating toward Israel's Arab-led political parties and would be open to the establishment of a Palestinian state.

But observers believe that message is exaggerated, and that the two-state solution is already dead.

"Support for Palestinian statehood has collapsed across most of the Jewish political spectrum, and permanent Israeli control over Palestinians has become normalized," Oppenheim pointed out. With the exception of one party, "all mainstream Jewish parties support, or at least acquiesce in, the settlement enterprise in some form and publicly oppose a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines."

In August this year, Eisenkot himself said that, "there is no Palestinian state, and no Palestinian state will be established under the government we form."

An Eisenkot-led government would, however, cooperate with more left-wing Israeli parties, which have previously supported a two-state solution. Any new coalition may also need the backing of Israel's Arab-led parties, who are currently thought to have increased their seats in parliament to around 19.

But as Mairav Zonszein, senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group, told the news agency Associated Press this week, "At best, [a new government] would be able to slow down the extremely crazy acceleration that we've seen in the last four years of every aspect of Israel's aggression in the occupied territories and inside Israel itself."

A less extreme government would tone down religious messaging, might be less demanding when it came to conditions on disarming Hamas in Gaza, and could potentially move forward with the next stage of the Gaza ceasefire, agreed to in late 2025, but barely implemented. It might also do more to contain settler violence in the West Bank.

"That's because [settler extremism] is a phenomenon that doesn't enjoy the support of the majority of Israelis, damages Israel's international reputation, and suppressing it is feasible," Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Policy Council, explained on social media.

"[A new Israeli government] would keep expanding the settlements and Palestinian statehood would remain taboo," Oppenheim wrote. "Without a diplomatic track with the Palestinians, further flare-ups of violence in the West Bank and Gaza are inevitable, destabilizing the region — and normalization with Saudi Arabia will remain off the table."

Saudi Arabia: Could anti-Netanyahu bloc bring normalization?

After the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and Israel's ensuing military campaign, which has resulted in at least 70,000 Palestinians killed and Gaza devastated, Saudi Arabia's conditions for normalization with Israel have hardened.

The country, hugely influential in the Muslim world, has put out several statements saying there could be no path to normalizing relations with Israel without some progress on Palestinian statehood.

Last week, at a meeting of foreign ministers from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, the Saudis co-signed a communique in which the four countries said Israel was "the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond."

But there is some cooperation between the two countries behind the scenes. Analysts say that if a government less hardline than Netanyahu's gets into power in Israel, it will be easier for countries like Saudi Arabia — but also the United Arab Emirates, Jordan and Egypt, which all have varying levels of backchannel cooperation and formal or informal contact with Israel — to admit to this kind of behind-the-scenes diplomacy.

Syria: Security agreement revived?

According to a study published last week by Syrian think tank, Etana, Israeli troops have come as far as 1,160 kilometers (721 miles) into Syria from the two countries' disputed border, occupied Syrian land as far as 400 kilometers from it and carried out 1,996 ground operations in southwest Syria between January and September this year.

Before elections this week there was no chance of any kind of withdrawal from Syria because it would have been seen as "defeat," Ksenia Svetlova, an associate fellow at Chatham House and a former member of the Israeli parliament, told online publication Syria in Transition this month. But if the anti-Netanyahu bloc gets into power, that could change, she suggested.

"A security agreement with Syria will become more probable, as many potential stakeholders [in a new, more centrist Israeli government] have spoken favorably about it in the past," noted Svetlova, who is also director of the Tel Aviv-based Regional Organization for Peace, Economics and Security, which works on Israeli-Palestinian-Arab partnerships. "However I do expect that it will take time as this government will be constantly attacked by the extreme right."

For months this year, Israel and Syrian diplomats negotiated a security agreement under the US' stewardship. But it came to nothing in late 2026 after Israel apparently refused to withdraw back to boundary lines established under a 1974 disengagement agreement.

Lebanon: More diplomacy wanted

Observers and media commentators in Lebanon say the Lebanese government would prefer to have Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc in power.

Lebanon and Israel are continuing to negotiate an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, where the Israelis claim they have established a "buffer zone" to facilitate their fight against Lebanese militia group, Hezbollah. The Lebanese argue the Israelis have in fact invaded their country.

And when it comes to negotiations around disarming Hezbollah and withdrawing Israeli troops, there's a perception in Lebanese political circles that Eisenkot would be easier to deal with than Netanyahu and his extremist allies.

This is despite the fact that Eisenkot is widely seen as the inventor of the so-called "Dahiyeh Doctrine," a military strategy that calls for asymmetric warfare in areas like Beirut's southern suburbs, where Hezbollah is based, to pressure both militants and their civilian support base.

A similar strategy is thought to be being implemented in southern Lebanon now, where whole villages continue to be razed by the Israeli military, even as active fighting has subsided.

Lebanese commentators are also optimistic that Eisenkot, former commander of the Israeli army, would have something in common with their own president, Joseph Aoun, who used to head Lebanon's armed forces.

"When Netanyahu was ousted from power between 2021 and 2022 by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid [now members of the camp led by Eisenkot], we were able to negotiate and conclude the maritime agreement," a Lebanese official told Lebanese daily, L'Orient Today, referring to a 2022 deal to share offshore territory.

entries.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy irked by US-Russia-China summit
entries.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced his concerns about a probable meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia next month. Plus, a localized truce appeared to be holding in the town of Oleshky.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's Zelenskyy irked by US-Russia-China summit

October 28, 2026

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced his concerns about a probable meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia next month. Plus, a localized truce appeared to be holding in the town of Oleshky.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that a planned meeting between Russia, China and the United States next month could present the three participants with an opportunity to redraw global spheres of influence.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," he said in comments to journalists on Wednesday, referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea , where Allied powers redrew the world map in the wake of the Second World War.

Putin raised idea of three-way summit with Trump: What to know

The Kremlin has previously indicated that preparations were underway for a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit next month.

The Wall Street Journal first broke the news about the three-way summit earlier this month and said that Trump had not agreed to attend the summit at the time.

But the Journal said Trump was open to the proposal — that had been raised by Putin — since he wanted to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.

"What China, Russia and the United States might discuss has not yet been clearly defined," Zelenskyy said, adding that "Russia wants this meeting more than anyone," warning against handing Moscow "another major diplomatic advantage."

For years now, Russia has been seeking a new agreement with Washington on European security architecture, and in particular an end to what Putin considers NATO's aggressive expansion towards Russia.

Putin has falsely repeatedly said Ukraine war was an act of self-defense

Putin continues to cast the ongoing invasion of Ukraine as a response to such a NATO threat – a position widely rejected in Kyiv and the rest of Europe.

Zelenskyy's warning came ahead of planned talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US envoys in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) next month.

No specific date has been set for the Abu Dhabi meeting, but Kyiv is keen for it to take place before the potential Russia-China-US summit.

Before that, it was also confirmed on Wednesday that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will travel to the United States for a meeting with G20 counterparts in Atlanta on October 30-31. 

Zelenskyy in Netherlands

Zelenskyy's remarks were released as he traveled to the Netherlands for meetings with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Dutch King Willem-Alexander in The Hague.

The Dutch government said on Wednesday it would provide Ukraine with €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) in non-military support over the next ⁠years.

Zelenskyy also held a phone call with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to thank him for an ​extra £10 ⁠billion ($13.29 billion/€11.94 billion) of support announced earlier ⁠on ​Wednesday.

"A truly ​strong very timely step coming right Russia needs to and ​feel that Ukraine will not be left ​alone to deal with the problems ⁠Russia ​is so ​eager to escalate," he wrote on social media.

But Ukraine's greatest assets in its defense against Russian aggression remain US Patriot air defense missiles, and Zelenskyy urged Washington to increase supplies.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been receiving 12 missiles a month this year but is being targeted with "150 ballistic missiles a month."

Oleshky truce holding for now, Zelenskyy says

Meanwhile on the battlefield, officials said a six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night.

The localized truce in the devastated town of Oleshky began on Tuesday and is due to last until Sunday, enabling a planned humanitarian operation to provide around 2,000 remaining residents with urgently needed food and medicine, and evacuate those who want to leave.

"We are grateful that they are organizing this possibility to evacuate people," said President Zelenskyy.

The plight of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region caught the attention of US first lady Melania Trump, who the White House said helped broker the humanitarian mission.

If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time in more than four-and-a-half years of fighting that both sides have observed a significant truce, with previous attempts quickly unraveling.

"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," said Ukraine's negotiator, Davyd ‌Arakhamia, on Tuesday, adding every step brings peace closer.

Drone attacks in Kharkiv, Belgorod — and off Bulgaria

Elsewhere, however, the war raged on with five people, including a four-year-old child, injured in a Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight.

In Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said air defenses had downed 531 Ukrainian drones on Tuesday night and into Wednesday morning, but local authorities in the Belgorod border region said one person was killed in a drone attack.

And in Sofia, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said three maritime drones struck a container ship in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria.

The crew evacuated the vessel and there were no immediate reports of casualties, according to Bulgarian state news agency BTA, but the incident took place as defense ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in Sofia for trilateral talks focused on Black Sea security.

"We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea ​and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas," said Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler.

"The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and ​immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels."

A series of drone attacks have occurred this month off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria. Russia has not taken responsibility, but suspicion has increasingly fallen on Moscow.

"The logic points in that direction," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told parliament earlier this month. "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in US, declares himself 'leader' of Brazil
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful leader of his country despite losing the presidential election runoff on Sunday. He and his family have fled to the US.
entries.content:
Brazil

Bolsonaro lands in US, declares himself 'leader' of Brazil

October 28, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful leader of his country despite losing the presidential election runoff on Sunday. He and his family have fled to the US.

Brazilian right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful leader of Brazil after landing in Miami with his family on Wednesday.

Bolsonaro fled Brazil after the Supreme Court asked him to hand over his passports so he couldn't leave the country.

The right-wing presidential candidate had not conceded defeat in Sunday's presidential election to rival, President Luiz Inacio "Lula"da Silva.

Bolsonaro lost elections on Sunday and alleged irregularities. His party has acknowledged the results of Sunday's elections and international observers have observed it was fair. 

In an initial open letter posted to X, Bolsonaro declared himself the "elected president." He then deleted the version and updated it with another letter in which he said he was the rightful "leader" of Brazil.

Bolsonaro faces criminal investigations into alleged financial crimes before the country's Supreme Court. But he has cast those investigations as a political witch hunt against his family by left-leaning justices.

"I want to say, not only to my 60 million voters but to the Brazilian people, that I am the leader and that the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a ​tyranny," he said in the updated version.

Asked by reporters at Joint Base Andrews about Bolsonaro's comments, US President Donald Trump declined to comment, reiterating earlier views on how it was "a very strange election."

The US State Department has said it will grant Bolsonaro and his family US visas. 

When did Bolsonaro arrive and how did he reach Miami?

Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters were seen disembarking a Gulfstream G400 plane and heading into the Miami-Opa Locka airport on Wednesday morning.

Their journey across the Americas had captured regional attention.

The quartet first flew into Argentina late on Tuesday, then took a private jet to the Ecuadorian city of Guayaquil. From there, they continued to Miami, in Florida.

Bolsonaro would lose his immunity from prosecution in February when his term in the Senate ends. On Monday, he had said in an Instagram post that he had no intention of leaving the country and that he would "hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."

According to the AFP news agency, Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship and so was able to travel despite his Brazilian and diplomatic passports being canceled.

Potential source of strain between Trump's US and Lula's Brazil

Bolsonaro's departure and his arrival in Florida — like his father Jair Bolsonaro before him after Brazil's previous presidential elections — could deepen a rift between the two most populous countries in the Americas. 

During the election campaign, incumbent leftist President Lula had accused the Donald Trump administration of colluding with the Bolsonaro family in a bid to help them return to power. 

After the election results, Trump appeared to question the integrity of the vote, saying he thought the extension to voting times was a "very bad look." He had also alleged in the past that Jair Bolsonaro was the victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.

Bolsonaro senior is now in jail in Brazil on charges of leading a conspiracy designed to keep him in power despite defeat in 2022's presidential election.

Edited by: Alex Berry

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Spanish train crash leaves 68 dead, PM Sanchez declares 3 days of mourning
entries.summary: Two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers collided south of Madrid. Spain's transport minister said one of the trains was told to continue its journey despite a "red signal" being in effect. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Published October 28, 2026last updated October 28, 2026

Two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers collided south of Madrid. Spain's transport minister said one of the trains was told to continue its journey despite a "red signal" being in effect. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • At least 68 people have died after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo
  • At least 100 people have been taken to hospital, several in critical condition
  • Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente says one of the trains was told to continue its journey even though all trains on the track had been ordered to stop
  • 378 passengers were on the Renfe train and another 147 on the Iryo train, according to Spanish media

Here are the latest updates from the high-speed train crash in Spain on Wednesday, October 28:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section More than 50 people discharged from hospital

More than 50 people discharged from hospital

Some 56 people who had been taken to hospital after the crash have now been discharged, the Health Ministry of Castilla-La Mancha region said, as cited by Spanish media.

This left 53 people still in hospital, according to the ministry.

Skip next section EU flags have been lowered to half-mast in solidarity with Spain

EU flags have been lowered to half-mast in solidarity with Spain

European Union flags have been lowered to half-mast outside the European Commission headquarters in Brussels as a marker of European solidarity.

The Commission said the flags were lowered after Spain declared three days of official mourning.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced the decision earlier this morning when he visited the crash site near Urda.

Wednesday's crash, which killed at least 68 people according to the latest updates, is the deadliest train disaster in the EU since 2013.

Skip next section Over 100 people in hospital following collision

Over 100 people in hospital following collision

At least 107 people remain admitted across hospitals in the region of Castilla-La Mancha following Wednesday's train crash, regional emergency services said in an update posted to X.

According to El Pais, of those, 18 were in critical condition.

The crash occurred close to the town of Urda, which is in the region of Castilla-La Mancha.

Skip next section WATCH: Train crash in Spain raises questions about rail safety

WATCH: Train crash in Spain raises questions about rail safety

At least 68 people were killed when a high-speed train slammed into a train that had stopped on the tracks.

The accident comes only nine months after a derailed train in the south of Spain led to 46 deaths.

Skip next section High-speed train crash in Spain: What do we know so far?

High-speed train crash in Spain: What do we know so far?

At least 68 people have died after a high-speed publicly-run Renfe train collided into the back of a privately-run Iryo train that was stopped farther along the tracks on the line between Madrid and the southern city of Seville.

The trains crashed just after 9 a.m. on Wednesday, between the towns of Mora and Orgaz, near Toledo. About 540 people were on the two trains, local officials said.

More than 100 remain injured.

Spain's train accident is the deadliest in Europe since 2013

Wednesday's accident was the second train disaster to have taken place in Spain this year and the deadliest train crash in Europe since 2013.

The train crash earlier this year in Spain also took place on the same line, with the collision near Cordoba having killed 46 people in January.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said in a televised address from near the accident site that "all of Spain" was in mourning.

He said the "terrible tragedy" would be investigated and vowed to address any failures that came to light.

Spain's Transportation Minister Oscar Puente said the crash resulted from an "inexplicable" decision by operators to have the high-speed train continue on its journey after a computer error had triggered a red signal closing down the stretch of track.

All major parties, apart from the far-right Vox party, cancelled their campaigning on Wednesday out of respect for the victims. Spaniards are set to head to the polls on November 29.

Skip next section Spain's 4 deadly train disasters this year: What to know

Spain's 4 deadly train disasters this year: What to know

The deadly train collision on Wednesday was the second high-speed rail crash this year. Spain's high-speed rail network, the largest in Europe, had gone without any fatal crashes since it opened in 1992. But there have also been fatal collisions on other parts of the network this year:

January 18: Derailment and collision near Cordoba kill 46

An Iryo train traveling from Malaga to Madrid derailed near Adamuz, in southern Spain, and collided with an oncoming Renfe train heading to Huelva.

46 people were killed and more than 100 injured. Investigators' preliminary findings indicated that a fracture in the rail appeared to predate the derailment.

January 20: Train strikes fallen wall near Barcelona

A commuter train crashed near Gelida, outside Barcelona, after a retaining wall collapsed onto the tracks during heavy rain.

One person was killed and 41 were injured, according to the Spanish government.

February 12: Motorist killed at a railroad crossing

A passenger train traveling from Madrid to Badajoz struck a car at a railroad crossing near Talavera de la Reina, in Toledo province.

The car's driver was killed. None of the 206 passengers aboard the train were injured, according to regional emergency services.

October 28: High-speed trains collide on line between Madrid and Seville

Two high-speed trains, both traveling from Madrid to Seville, collided near Urda, in Toledo province, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, regional authorities said.

Skip next section Spanish cup football matches suspended after fatal train accident

Spanish cup football matches suspended after fatal train accident

Spain's football federation (RFEF) has suspended over 20 Spanish cup (Copa del Rey) fixtures scheduled for Wednesday out of respect for the victims of the deadly train crash earlier in the day.

"As a sign of respect and solidarity with all the victims of the tragic train accident … the RFEF has suspended the 24 matches corresponding to the first round of the Copa del Rey initially scheduled to be played during this afternoon and evening," the RFEF said in a statement.

Five top division teams (Levante, Alaves, Valencia, Celta Vigo and Real Betis) were due to play their first-round matches on Wednesday — but Spanish giants Real Madrid, Atletico Madrid and Barcelona aren't due to enter the competition until the round-of-32 in December.

Several Spanish football clubs have expressed condolences and solidarity on social media.

"FC Barcelona expresses its deepest condolences to the victims of the serious railway accident," wrote the Catalonia-based team. "The club wishes to convey its support and solidarity to the families and friends of the victims and to wish all those injured a speedy recovery."

Real Madrid also published a statement expressing "deepest sorrow" and extending condolences.

As it stands, Thursday's Copa del Rey fixtures (featuring La Liga sides Athletic Bilbao, Osasuna, Deportivo A Coruna, Getafe and FC Sevilla) are still set to go ahead.

New dates for the postponed Wednesday games have not yet been announced.

Skip next section Spain to observe 3 days of mourning after rail collision

Spain to observe 3 days of mourning after rail collision

Spain will observe three days of mourning after the death of at least 68 people in a high-speed train collision on Wednesday, Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced.

"All of Spain is in mourning," he said from the scene of the crash in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, adding that it was "not acceptable for a country like Spain" to suffer two such disasters in the same year.

Skip next section Renfe train was told to continue journey despite red signal, transport minister says

Renfe train was told to continue journey despite red signal, transport minister says

The Renfe high-speed train that crashed into another stationary train had been told to continue its journey "as normal" despite the fact that all trains on the section of track in Toledo province had been told to stop, Spain's Transport Minister Oscar Puente has said.

Puente told a press conference at the ADIF control center in Madrid that the control system at the train station in Urda had failed due to a computer error.

That failure meant that a 63-kilometer section of track had no control system, which triggered an automatic stop, or "red signal," for all rail traffic on the parts of the track affected.

Operators at the control center ADIF, the company that is responsible for managing and maintaining Spain's railway infrastructure, took over communications.

"At 8:36 a.m. the Renfe train was told to resume its journey 'with normality'," Puente explained, a decision he described as "inexplicable."

He said that between that time and the moment of impact at 8:53, the Renfe train had traveled about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles), likely reaching a speed of over 100 kilometers (60 miles) per hour.

During the press conference, Puente refused to respond to questions about whether he would resign in the wake of the crash, saying his attention was on clarifying the circumstances that led to the crash and supporting the victims.

Skip next section EU leaders send condolences, support to Spain after crash

EU leaders send condolences, support to Spain after crash

Senior European Union leaders Ursula von der Leyen and Kaja Kallas have sent their condolences to the victims of the high-speed rail crash and their families.

European Commission President von der Leyen said "Europe mourns with you."

Kaja Kallas, the EU's foreign policy and security chief, said she had spoken to Spain's Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares to convey her "profound condolences following the tragic accident."

"Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives. I wish a swift recovery to the injured and strength to all those affected," Kallas said.

European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho, meanwhile, said the bloc was "ready to help Spain if needed."

Skip next section Spain's PM Sanchez heading to crash site

Spain's PM Sanchez heading to crash site

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is traveling to Urda, where two high-speed trains collided.

At least 64 people have been killed, while more than 80 people have been injured in one of the worst rail accidents in Spain's history.

In a post on X, the Moncloa Palace, the prime minister's official residence, said Sanchez was heading to Urda to "support the work of the emergency teams and to convey his support to those affected and their families."

"The priority is to attend to the victims and ensure the maximum coordination between administrations," it added.

Skip next section Spanish royals 'saddened and distressed' over accident

Spanish royals 'saddened and distressed' over accident

Spain's royal family has issued a statement following the deadly train crash in Toledo.

In a post on X, the royals said they are "deeply saddened and distressed" over the accident.

"We share the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt thoughts to the injured and everyone affected."

Spain's King Felipe VI, meanwhile, told reporters in Valencia that he was cutting short his military training exercise at the Jaime I Military Base to return to Madrid to monitor the emergency response to the accident.

Felipe added that he had already been in touch with the regional Castilla-La Mancha president.

Skip next section Do we know what caused the accident?

Do we know what caused the accident?

A train operated by the private Iryo consortium was reportedly told to stop by rail infrastructure manager ADIF due to a faulty signal, a person briefed on the disaster told the Reuters news agency.

Government officials have not confirmed what caused the train crash, and neither Renfe nor Iryo have commented on the cause.

DW has spoken to Nick Kingsley, the executive editor of the Railway Gazette International, about what might have caused the crash, the second fatal accident to hit Spain's high-speed rail network this year.

Kingsley described it as "a dark day for the Spanish rail industry" and said there would be "profound questions asked" as to how this accident occurred.

While he cautioned that it was still too early to speculate, Kingsley said: "The key point with high-speed railway is you design safety systems and especially signalling and train control systems such that the trains do not crash. This should never happen."

He said investigators would be looking into whether there are any similarities with the fatal accident in January.

"The fact that these two accidents happened in the same year when we had 30+ years without a single fatal accident on a high-speed rail network anywhere in the world, to now have this happen twice in one year in the same country is quite shocking," Kingsley told DW.

What are investigators going to be looking at?

"If reports that one crashed into the back of the other are confirmed, that will raise questions about the protection of those sections of track," Kingsley said.

He explained that the "fundamental principle of railway operation is that you have a signalling system that is designed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track. This is a fundamental tenet of railway operation."

Kingsley added that it will take a long time, possibly several weeks or even months, "to establish a definitive sequence of events."

Skip next section Death toll climbs to 64 — regional government

Death toll climbs to 64 — regional government

The death toll from the accident has risen to at least 64, a spokesperson for Castilla-La Mancha's regional president, Emiliano Garcia-Page, has said.

At least 58 people were injured, many of them seriously, officials have confirmed.

The toll has risen several times during the day, with the possibility remaining that it could still go up.

Skip next section Regional president: 'We expect more deaths'

Regional president: 'We expect more deaths'

The president of the regional Castilla-La Mancha government, Emiliano Garcia-Page, has told reporters at the scene of the accident that at least 80 people were lightly or moderately injured as a result of the crash.

"There are also fewer who were seriously injured, so we unfortunately do expect more deaths," Garcia-Page said.

He added that the priority is to treat the injured and move them to hospital.

"We are in the heart of the emergency, so the priority is to attend to the injured, the dead and the victims' families," he said.

Help is arriving from neighboring regions, the president said, as he urged people to remain calm and to allow the emergency services to deal with the accident.

He also refused to speculate on what caused the accident.

"I'm not the one who should comment on the causes, that should come from judicial authorities. The judicial authorities should be the ones to establish the causes of this incident," he said.

entries.title: Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?
entries.summary: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have taken their latest peace push directly to Tehran. Officially, it was to avert a new military escalation, but their diplomatic outreach can also be seen as a warning to Iran.
entries.content:
Iran

Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?

October 28, 2026

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have taken their latest peace push directly to Tehran. Officially, it was to avert a new military escalation, but their diplomatic outreach can also be seen as a warning to Iran.

Amid rising fear that the US and Israel are preparing to launch new attacks on Iran after the US midterm election on November 3, three major Middle Eastern powers delivered a coordinated diplomatic message directly to Tehran.

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Iran to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials in Tehran this Monday. The three envoys serve as representatives for the Mecca defense pact — a military alliance of Islamabad, Riyad and Ankara, which was officially set up this summer.

Saudi Arabia said ⁠the ⁠trip aims to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation." Details on the agenda, however, remain scarce.

A senior Pakistani official cited by the Reuters news agency said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, in addition to US-Iran talks, Houthi rebels' attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade.

Another official said Pakistan's Munir presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something both to Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar acting as mediators. The source told Reuters US President Donald Trump previously gave Munir the go-ahead to try diplomacy.

Tehran presents the meeting as a success

Iran hailed the "very positive atmosphere" during the Tehran talks, even though no breakthroughs were officially announced.

"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region."

Rezaei argued that regional security should be built by countries in West Asia themselves and without outside intervention.

A day later, Rezaei reportedly met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media said Khamenei called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace."

Meanwhile, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian travelled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, with Pezeshkian and the emir also discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz.

These and other diplomatic contacts were framed by Tehran as evidence that the US is unable to diplomatically isolate the Iranian regime.

Are Turkey and Pakistan closing ranks with Saudi Arabia?

The united front presented by the three nations in Tehran, however, can also be seen as a show of force for the new Mecca defense alliance. It comes as the Saudis grow increasingly wary of the attacks on Saudi infrastructure launched by the Iran-allied Houthi militants.

Under the terms of the Mecca agreement, an outside attack on one of the member states is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. The visit also came on the same day as Egypt's parliament agreeing to give military help to Ryad and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, in addition to the looming threat of the US and Israel.

"The presence of the three senior representatives at the same time sent the message that these countries are acting as a bloc," Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW.

Saudi Arabia has long been regarded as Iran's archrival in region. It has used its enormous wealth to counter Iran's influence, and now it can, at least in theory, also count on Pakistan's nuclear capability, and Turkey's conventional military strength.

At the same time, Dorbeiki argued that the Mecca pact is primarily designed for deterrence rather than offensive war. And having a defense pact does not mean its members want to fight Iran.

Dorbeiki believes the message from the bloc could therefore work in two directions: It can provide mediation, but continued escalation could also alter that position.

Ryad pushing for a 'diplomatic solution'

Saudi Arabia faces the most immediate dilemma. Further Houthi attacks have damaged its infrastructure and economy, but a wider war with Iran could threaten the investment and development projects at the heart of Riyadh's economic strategy.

"For Saudi Arabia, both the current situation and a war with Iran carry serious costs," Dorbeiki said. "Its preferred route is, therefore, a diplomatic solution."

Moreover, Pakistan has spent months mediating between Washington and Tehran, and has important relations with both. A direct conflict would also distract Islamabad from its long-standing security concerns involving India.

Turkey is a NATO member, but Dorbeiki said direct military support for Iran against the United States is highly improbable. The fact that Ankara sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin rather than its foreign or defense minister also suggests a cautious approach.

Iran pursues diplomacy while preparing for fighting

Ali Asghar Shafieian, media advisor for Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, also rejected the perspective that the Mecca pact representatives were trying to present Tehran with an ultimatum.

He told DW that the three countries may also have wanted to demonstrate their own growing coordination, while showing that Iran remains part of regional diplomacy.

"You cannot conclude from this meeting alone that it was an ultimatum before an attack," Shafieian said.

He also noted that Iran, just like the US and Israel, could prepare for the possibility of further conflict while maintaining negotiations.

"Just as they use the opportunity to strengthen their military and defensive capabilities, Iran does the same," he said, adding that an agreement remains possible if Iran's political standing and what Tehran describes as its national dignity are respected.

Diplomatic game continues

Dorbeiki argued that Iran is following a familiar strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding real-world commitments.

The Houthi rebels are central to Tehran's calculation.

Tehran has not publicly offered the kind of guarantees over Houthi attacks that Riyadh would want. Dorbeiki believes Iran could seek to trade influence over such the attacks for concessions such as an end to US military pressure and broader steps toward ending the war.

The only apparent outcome of the Tehran meeting is to keep talking. For Iran, that might be enough of a signal that it is still a diplomatic partner rather than an enemy.

Edited by: Shamil Shams

entries.title: Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?
entries.summary: Young people in Germany will take to the streets this weekend to demand education and action on climate change. Politicians warn that the protests could become violent, as in France, but the situations are different.
entries.content:
Germany

Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?

October 28, 2026

Young people in Germany will take to the streets this weekend to demand education and action on climate change. Politicians warn that the protests could become violent, as in France, but the situations are different.

As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities.

CDU: 'We must prevent scenes like those in France at all costs'

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.

Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.

Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."

Concerns over internationally coordinated far-left extremists

In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.

Koos: 'Not driven by anger as in France'

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

Greens express understanding for the protests

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries.

"Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said.

"And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead with more than 80% of votes counted
entries.summary: While partial results show the pro-Netanyahu bloc ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, the final tally could take days. Neither grouping is expected to win a majority, with tough coalition talks ahead. Follow DW.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead as count continues

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026

While partial results show the pro-Netanyahu bloc ahead of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, the final tally could take days. Neither grouping is expected to win a majority, with tough coalition talks ahead. Follow DW.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israel's election turnout was the highest in decades
  • As of 12:30 p.m. local time, just over 84.5% of the vote was counted with a Likud-led bloc holding a lead
  • At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
  • Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot both say they're ready to form government
  • Neither party is expected to win an outright majority, with difficult coalition talks expected in the weeks ahead

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and the following days:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

UN rights chief: Next government should 'change course massively'

The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, Volker Türk, told reporters in New York that he hopes a new Israeli government will "change course massively" and respect international law. 

"The message is: don't continue the current course of warfare where you think you are above international law, because I think that's what we have frankly seen in the current environment," Türk said, as relayed by the AFP news agency.

"Israel has its obligations under international law, international humanitarian law, international human rights law, and they need to respect them," he said. "And I hope that the next government will do precisely that and change course massively."

Türk also said in a statement on Monday that Israel's operation in recent days in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron raised serious concerns about "unnecessary and disproportionate" use of force.

He said that more than 2,000 people had been displaced, with homes and commercial property destroyed and free movement impeded by the lockdown.

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law," Türk said. "Threats to empty and erase entire neighborhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing."

Skip next section 'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

'Arab Israelis have trusted democracy,' Greens' Omid Nouripour tells DW

Omid Nouripour, one of the deputy speakers in Germany's Bundestag parliament, has told DW that the high turnout in Israel was a testament to the strength of the country's democracy.

"For now, of course, we do not know what the coalition-building will look like, but the people have put their trust in democracy," Nouripour said. "Above all, Arab Israelis have trusted democracy and gone to the polls in droves."

Speaking to DW's Rosalia Romaniec, as he accompanies German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier on his state visit to China, Nouripour also said that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's and other right-wing parties' religiously-charged campaign strategy appeared to have backfired.

"This big campaign from Netanyahu's camp, first and foremost against the Arab Israelis, has on the one hand mobilized people to such an extent that there is no longer a majority for this camp," he said.

Nouripour, a former Green party co-leader, has been a Bundestag member for 20 years. Born in Tehran, his family moved from Iran to Germany when he was a teenager.

Skip next section WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

WATCH: Early Israeli election results point to deadlock

Israel's election has produced no clear winner, leaving both Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot short of a path to power. Israel could now be facing weeks of political uncertainty.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

IN DEPTH: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors?

A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say.

Some small positives may be possible though.

Read DW's full report on what might change for Arab countries after Israel's election.

Skip next section GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

GRAPHIC — Knesset seats by party, and by bloc

Skip next section Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

Election commission says almost half a million 'double envelope' ballots still to be counted

The Central Elections Commission (CEC) estimates that there are still between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double envelope" ballots to count, according to Israeli media.

These are cast primarily by soldiers, prisoners and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as others unable to vote at their designated polling stations.

This estimate is lower than the CEC's previous prediction of around 600,000 but it remains subject to change.

Such ballots are still being received and processed, and officials also have to double-check that the individuals sending them in have not also voted at a physical polling station on election day.

Because of these complications, they tend to be among the last votes to be counted.

A full vote count is tentatively expected by tomorrow afternoon, although the official finalized results will only follow on November 4.

If the CEC's estimated range is roughly correct, this group of ballots would equate to not very far shy of 10% of the total number of votes cast. As such, they have at least the theoretical potential to impact the seat distribution quite considerably.

Skip next section President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.

"I will receive  the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions." 

Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.

"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments. 

Skip next section Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.

The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.

Neither bloc is set to receive the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.

Right-wing Jewish parties in Israel have traditionally refused to cooperate with Arab parties, and Netanyahu said on Wednesday doing so would be "treasonous."
